Facebook has a lot more ads placed in the newsfeed but it wasn't that way early on, and if it's about ads why doesn't Reddit use more to become profitable?
Why was Facebook able to make such massive profits and Reddit has not for doing almost the same thing?

Reddit doesn't acquire any personal information, except very roughly your interests. But those interests can't be coupled to a name or location, only to your account (and maybe an IP). Even an emailadress is optional. Personal information can be used to target adds, and it can be sold. Even outside facebook, it's very valuable to know the interests of a certain user so companies can use adds in an effective way.

Also, because of the anonymity on reddit, people can easily switch accounts, or even websites. This "new reddit" (voat) has already remarkably many users. And why? Because reddit decided to use some (compared to facebook) very minor censorship. Now think of all the shit facebook has gotten away with, and there's still no serious alternative. People have a personal account, are tied to real life friends etcetera. You can't just switch on your own, so in the end nobody does. Facebook users are pretty much tied to the website. I'm pretty confident that in 5 years, Facebook will still stand as it is (or larger), while reddit might experience a serious downfall. Might, but it's way more likely than for facebook.

An "economy of scale" exists when it is cheaper to make money the bigger you are.

Most companies have "producer-side economies of scale." This means that the more employees you have, the more tools you have, the more efficient you can be. Time Magazine and CNN have this kind of economy of scale.

You can also have consumer-side economies of scale. That means the more customers you have, the better it is for each of your customers. Office formats have this. Facebook have this (it's more useful if 2 friends are on it than 1, and more useful if 20 are than 10). Reddit... kind of has it.

Unfortunately, Reddit is much much smaller than Facebook. So way less consumer-side economies of scale AND less producer-side economies of scale.

You can fight this by giving up (I think that's what Reddit is doing -- the purges seem to be trying to turn it into a magazine instead of a social network) or embracing a niche (that's what Voat is doing -- emphasizing it is for free speech, and that those customers would be happy in a smaller, freer community).

My 2 cents.
